title: increasing and decreasing patterns, using tables and charts

lesson.title: Patterns That Grow and Patterns That Shrink

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Let's start with something real. Maya lives in Kelowna and she's saving for a bike. Every Saturday she puts four dollars into her jar. After one week she has four dollars, after two weeks eight dollars, after three weeks twelve dollars, after four weeks sixteen dollars. Her mom asks, how much will you have after ten weeks? Instead of guessing, Maya writes her money in a table. A table is like a tidy row of drawers, one drawer for each week, so nothing gets mixed up.

Now here's the magic trick, and it's the whole lesson. Look at the jump between one number and the next. From four to eight is four. From eight to twelve is four. From twelve to sixteen is four. The same jump every single time! When the numbers keep getting bigger by the same amount, we call it an increasing pattern. The size of the jump has a name too. We call it the rule. Maya's rule is add four.

visual.caption: Going up by 4 each week — a steady climb

steps.say: Once you know the rule, you can keep the pattern going forever. Sixteen plus four is twenty, so week five is twenty dollars. Twenty plus four is twenty-four, so week six is twenty-four dollars. Do you notice these are the numbers you say when you skip count by four? Look at them lit up on the hundred chart. That's what an increasing pattern looks like — steady, even hops, never a wobbly one.

But not every pattern grows. Some patterns shrink, and those are just as useful. Maya's dad puts fifty dollars on his transit card. Each week he taps six dollars for the SkyTrain. After one week he has forty-four dollars left, then thirty-eight, then thirty-two, then twenty-six. The numbers get smaller by six every time. That's a decreasing pattern, and its rule is subtract six.

visual.caption: Dollars left on the transit card — going down by 6

steps.say: Let's try a real BC one together. Scientists count the rainbow trout in a small lake each spring. In two thousand nineteen they counted nine hundred fish. Then seven hundred fifty, then six hundred, then four hundred fifty. Let's find the jump. Nine hundred take away seven hundred fifty is one hundred fifty. Seven hundred fifty take away six hundred is one hundred fifty. Six hundred take away four hundred fifty is one hundred fifty. Same jump every year, and it's going down. So the rule is subtract one hundred fifty.

visual.caption: Trout counted in the lake — the line slides downhill

steps.say: Now use the rule to look into the future. Four hundred fifty take away one hundred fifty is three hundred, so in two thousand twenty-three the scientists would expect about three hundred trout. See how helpful that is? The table told them the fish were disappearing, so they could stock the lake with young trout before it was too late. That's why we learn patterns — a table can warn you about something before it happens.

visual.caption: The predicted number for next year

steps.say: One last example, a little trickier because it doesn't start at zero. You plant a bean seedling for your class garden and it's already twelve centimetres tall. It grows five centimetres each week. Twelve plus five is seventeen. Seventeen plus five is twenty-two. Twenty-two plus five is twenty-seven. Twenty-seven plus five is thirty-two. Even though it started at twelve, the jumps are all the same, so it's still an increasing pattern with the rule add five.

visual.caption: Height of the bean plant in centimetres

steps.say: So here's the whole secret in one breath. Put your numbers in a table, then look at the jump between them. If the jump is the same each time, you have found the rule. Going up means increasing, going down means decreasing, and once you know the rule you can tell what happens next. You're a pattern detective now!

visual.caption: One hop of the rule: add 5

lesson.answer: Line the numbers up in a table, find the same-sized jump between them — that jump is the rule, and it tells you what comes next.

practice.question: Liam puts sixty dollars on his school lunch card. Each week he spends seven dollars. Make a table showing how much is left after week one, two, three and four. Is this an increasing or a decreasing pattern, what is the rule, and how much is left after week five?
practice.answer: Week 1: $53, Week 2: $46, Week 3: $39, Week 4: $32. It is a decreasing pattern and the rule is subtract 7. After week five there is $25 left, because 32 minus 7 equals 25.
